items.heading: Video 3.1 |  Content Creation
items.paragraph: This video explores three of the ten key areas where GenAI can assist: drafting content, brainstorming ideas, proofreading and editing. Hands-on demos and exercises allow participants to practice these applications.

items.title: Audio description transcript – Content Creation
items.description:
[Visual description]: Text appears: The InnovateUS Logo.

[Visual description]: Title card: Responsible AI for Public Professionals: Using GenAI in Government.

[Visual description]: Title card: Drafting, Brainstorming, and Editing.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Ariana Escanlante, presenter, InnovateUS.

In this video, we will look at how you can streamline how you work.

By the end of this video, you'll have:

[Visual description]: Title card: Video Goals.

A solid understanding of ten key ways you can use GenAI

Tried using GenAI to do those tasks

A framework for integrating GenAI into your work

We encourage you to pause the video and experiment alongside us with approved tools.

Again, we are not endorsing any one tool, just encouraging you to try for yourself to understand what they can and cannot do.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Disclaimer: Always review and fact-check GenAI-generated content.

Remember: human oversight is always crucial. Always review and fact-check GenAI-generated content. Research has shown that people all too often follow GenAI’s suggestions without critical scrutiny, even when it's wrong.

Let's explore ten common tasks we can now do more easily when we know how to use AI well.

[Visual description]: Title card: 1: Drafting.

Facing a daunting blank page? Let GenAI kick-start your writing. 

[Visual description]: Text appears: Disclaimer: The commercial tools mentioned in this course are for illustrative purposes and do not imply endorsement by InnovateUS.

Whether it's a press release, policy memo, job description, website content, or phone tree responses, GenAI can produce a preliminary draft when given a bit of direction.

[Visual description]: An AI tool is being asked to generate a formal email draft to invite members of the public to a government hearing.

GenAI can also create a first draft of an image — for example, an urban planning illustration for your event blog post or presentation.

[Visual description]: The AI generates an image showing a group of people meeting while standing over a map model with information on the government hearing.

[Visual description]: Title card: 2: Brainstorming.

Stuck on a project or a section of a policy memo? GenAI can play the role of brainstormer. Unlike a simple web search, you can have a real conversation with GenAI — generate ideas, refine them, and keep pushing until you find something useful. Remember: if you don't like the first response, keep prompting. You can have a dialogue — push back, ask for more, ask it to narrow down.

[Visual description]: The AI generates responses to the asked questions and keeps up the conversation to help the user.

[Visual description]: Title card: 2: Editing & Proofreading.

GenAI can catch errors and help you improve the clarity of your writing and the strength of your argument. It can help you correct your grammar, propose structural changes, or rewrite text, for example, for web pages or press releases.

[Visual description]: An AI tool is being tasked to rewrite a paragraph of a memo to heighten the clarity and to make the text accessible for a 9th-grade reading level.

Remember if practicing with free tools, only use publicly available content.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Warning. Do not include any personally identifiable information (PII) or sensitive information in your request.

In our next video, we'll keep going with our list of ten tasks.

items.title: What is the benefit of experimenting with multiple generative AI platforms?

answers.title: To ensure you are using the most expensive platform
answers.feedback: Spending more on a platform does not necessarily mean better results.

answers.title: To discover which platform generates the most content

answers.title: To find the platform that best aligns with your needs
To determine which platform has the most users
answers.feedback: The number of users does not necessarily indicate the best fit for your specific use case.

items.title: When using generative AI to draft or modify content, what are the key responsibilities of the human user? (Select all that apply)

answers.title: A. Reviewing the AI-generated content for accuracy
B. Fact-checking the information provided by the AI
C. Disclosing the use of AI in their work
D. Accepting the AI-generated content without modification

items.feedbackIncorrect: The correct answers are A, B, and C. When using generative AI to draft or modify content, the key responsibilities of the human user include reviewing the AI-generated content for accuracy, fact-checking the information provided by the AI, and disclosing the use of AI in their work. Users should not accept the AI-generated content without review and potential modification.

items.heading: Video 3.2 |  Content Analysis
items.paragraph: This video explores three of the ten key areas where GenAI can assist: summarizing, labeling, and researching. Hands-on demos and exercises allow participants to practice these applications.

items.title: Audio description transcript - Summarising and Synthesising
items.description:
[Visual description]: Text appears: The InnovateUS Logo.

[Visual description]: Title card: Responsible AI for Public Professionals: Using GenAI in Government.

[Visual description]: Title card: Summarising and Synthesising.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Ariana Escanlante, presenter, InnovateUS.

Welcome back! We're discussing ten ways to use GenAI in government work. While our first three tasks were about creating content, let's look at content analysis.

[Visual description]: Title card: 4: Summarizing.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Disclaimer: The commercial tools mentioned in this course are for illustrative purposes and do not imply endorsement by InnovateUS.

In government, we often deal with large amounts of information: lengthy PDFs, voluminous regulations,  notes from countless meetings. GenAI excels at distilling it.

[Visual description]: An AI tool is tasked with summarising a multi-page PDF document into 200 words.

You can also generate summaries from audio files. Platforms like Zoom, Teams, Wudpecker, and Otter.ai all offer AI-powered transcription and summarization features.

[Visual description]: The Otter AI interface is shown as it transcribes a public meeting from an audio file.

[Visual description]: Title card: 5: Categorizing & Labeling.

Sometimes we don't need to summarize but to sort — like when you have a large number of resident comments from a public consultation. GenAI is very good at classifying. You can provide a set of text, give it guidance on the label types you want, and ask it to sort them.

[Visual description]: An AI tool labels a set of public comments by their sentiment.

[Visual description]: Title card: 6: Synthesizing Information Across Sources.

Often, you have information from multiple sources and need to extract insights. Try uploading multiple documents and ask for a comparison.

[Visual description]: An AI tool is asked to compare 7 documents and to summarise their overlap.

See you in the next video, where we'll wrap up our ten examples.

items.heading: Video 3.3 |  Conversational, Coding, and Data Analysis Uses
items.paragraph: The remaining four key areas are covered: engaging in role-play for preparation, accelerating learning, coding, and formatting information. The video emphasizes the importance of understanding the underlying processes and reviewing outputs for accuracy.

items.title: Audio description transcript - Conversational, Coding, and Data Analysis Uses
items.description:
[Visual description]: Text appears: The InnovateUS Logo.

[Visual description]: Title card: Responsible AI for Public Professionals: Using GenAI in Government.

[Visual description]: Title card: Conversational, Coding, and Data Analysis Uses.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Ariana Escanlante, presenter, InnovateUS.

Welcome back! In our discussion of ten ways you can use GenAI, we've covered content creation and content analysis. 

[Visual description]: Content Creation is shown as a woman sitting behind a computer streaming out a torrent of music notes, scripts, and videos. Content Analysis is shown as a torrent of creative information being funneled into a lightbulb held by a woman.

But these tools are also great at teaching, especially when we use them to ask us questions.

[Visual description]: An image of an AI tutor breaking down a math problem to teach a user.

[Visual description]: Title card: 7: Role Playing.

GenAI can assist by adopting a role. 

[Visual description]: Title card: Sample Prompt.

[Visual description]: The following prompt is presented to an AI: "I have a public event coming up where I will need to answer questions from the audience about my organization's recent policy change to rezone the 300 block of downtown.

Attached is a 2-page document with further information about the project. Pretend you are a resident of the downtown area who is angry about the proposal. Please ask a question and engage with me in a back-and-forth dialogue. Afterwards, please provide constructive feedback on how I answered."

You can steer it to act as, for example, an audience member at a town hall, a skeptical reporter, or a tough interviewer. With a clearly defined role and context, it can engage in dialogue, ask probing questions, and offer structured feedback on your responses. Some platforms also support voice interaction, allowing you to speak with it and receive in-character replies.

[Visual description]: The AI responds to the prompt and then uses the voice interaction feature to speak with the AI.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Disclaimer: The commercial tools mentioned in this course are for illustrative purposes and do not imply endorsement by InnovateUS.

A note of caution: steering shapes tone, perspective, and style, but it does not ensure factual accuracy. Asking it to sound like a professor does not make its answers more reliable. Use steering to guide how the output is framed, and verify important claims independently.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Sound like a professor does not equal think like a professor.

To be clear: GenAI is never a replacement for actual engagement with residents. It can't tell you what people actually think. But it can help you be a better conversation starter.

[Visual description]: Title card: 8: Tutor. 

Often, we don't need GenAI to give us answers — we need it to generate questions: for witnesses, for the public, to prepare for a meeting, or to test our understanding of a topic. 

[Visual description]: An AI is asked to write a ten-question test to test a user's understanding of Gen-AI.

With the right instructions, GenAI can produce questions and act as a coach or tutor that can help you simplify complicated topics, prepare a study guide and quiz you, and suggest what to study next.

[Visual description]: The user asks the AI to give the questions one by one and to give feedback it complies and begins the test.

[Visual description]: Title card: 9: Coding.

As with text, you can use Generative AI to write and analyze computer code.  These tools can significantly increase the speed at which programmers work. 

More importantly, they are lowering the barrier to entry, making it easier for non-experts to start building simple applications.

You may hear this described as “vibe coding,” using natural language to generate working code without deep programming expertise. 

[Visual description]: An AI is asked to analyse a piece of code, explain what it does, and to identify bugs, security vulnerabilities, performance issues, and areas where the code can be simplified.

While you might not build a fully functional government system, you can use GenAI to prototype new services and tools.

In this demo, we write a prompt, asking an AI assistant to build a web application for an online renewable energy grant application. The prompt requests a form to collect user information, logic to check eligibility, and storage of submitted applications.

[Visual description]: The AI responds to the prompt in a set of blocks of code separated by both their programming language and utility.

The AI produces a structured block of code – not a finished product, but a solid start that a developer could immediately build on.

GenAI can also review existing code to flag potential security issues, generate documentation, and create test cases. As with any coding task, you still need enough understanding to evaluate and validate the output.

[Visual description]: Title card: 10: Data Analysis.

You can use GenAI to analyze and manipulate data — both text and numbers — making it useful even for those of us who aren't data scientists.

[Visual description]: A complex spreadsheet titled Raw Fictional U.S. Public Service Requests - Deliberately Messy Data is shown and uploaded to an AI. 

We upload a ridership spreadsheet and generate a visualization of year-over-year bus trends. Next, we can ask for the right Excel formula to extract phone numbers. Then, we can clean and properly format a list of names into a structured table, catching and fixing missed details like a middle initial.

[Visual description]: The AI analyses the spreadsheet and gives advice regarding the data.

You need to review for errors. But the time saved from using these tools will more than make up for the time spent reviewing and verifying.

[Visual description]: A list titled Ten common tasks is shown, which lists: Drafting, Brainstorming, Editing and Proofreading, Summarizing, Categorizing and Labeling, Synthesizing Information Across Sources, Role-Playing, Coaching and Question Generation, Coding, and Data Analysis.

For every task in this list, GenAI gets you most of the way there, fast. Your expertise gets you the rest of the way. This combination is more powerful than either approach independently.

[Visual description]: Text appears: You plus GenAI is greater than You OR GenAI.

Now that we've covered the ten ways you can use GenAI in your day-to-day work, let’s talk about getting the most from these tools.

items.title: Audio description transcript – Tips For Using GenAI
items.description:
[Visual description]: Text appears: The InnovateUS Logo.

[Visual description]: Title card: Responsible AI for Public Professionals: Using GenAI in Government.

[Visual description]: Title card: Tips For Using GenAI.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Ariana Escanlante, presenter, InnovateUS.

Welcome back. We’ve covered ten common tasks you can do with Generative AI. Now let’s turn to four practical tips for getting started and integrating these tools into your work.

[Visual description]: Title card: Tip 1: Starts with internal tasks.

[Visual description]: Text appears: Disclaimer: The commercial tools mentioned in this course are for illustrative purposes and do not imply endorsement by InnovateUS.

When you're getting started with GenAI, begin with low-risk internal uses. Help yourself prepare for a meeting, write a first draft of an email to a colleague, or summarize a document for your own use.

[Visual description]: An AI is asked to help prepare a user for a meeting by creating a short briefing with the key issue, questions they should ask, points to discuss, and three possible next steps.

This gives you time to learn how to guide these tools effectively before you put them to work on something the public will see.

[Visual description]: Title card: Tip 2: Break down big jobs.

GenAI works best on specific, well-defined tasks — not sprawling projects. If you need to develop a new policy, break it into parts: research, drafting, stakeholder outreach, data analysis. Then use GenAI to help with each step along the way.

[Visual description]: The mentioned parts are arranged in a mind map around the goal of developing a new policy.

[Visual description]: Title card: Tip 3: set realistic expectations.

When applying GenAI to a task, think of it like a brand-new hire. You wouldn't immediately assign a complex project to someone just starting out. You'd start with a task that can be explained quickly and clearly — like proofreading a draft. The more experienced you get at using these tools, the more complex the tasks you can assign.

[Visual description]: Title card: Tip 4: Experiment, then evaluate.

The more you try these tools, the better you'll get at using them. The best results come from practice and experimentation. Stay in the driver's seat: GenAI is a great helper, so long as you actively evaluate what it produces.

[Visual description]: Title card: Learning Outcomes.

Hopefully we have

Expanded your understanding of GenAI's capabilities

Illustrated ten uses: from writer to role-player, tutor to coder

and Outlined four tips for getting the most from these tools

Next up: a deep dive into writing prompts.

answers.title: Use AI to complete the entire project at once
answers.feedback: Attempting to use AI to complete an entire large project at once is not the most effective approach.

answers.title: Break the project down into smaller, specific tasks
Avoid using AI for large projects altogether

answers.title: Expect AI to replace all human involvement in the project
answers.feedback: AI is a tool to assist with tasks, not a complete replacement for human involvement in a project.

answers.title: A brand new trainee
A complete replacement for human workers
